subject: Renal
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has sudden colicky left flank pain radiating to the groin and hematuria. CT shows a hyperdense renal stone. Urine microscopy shows envelope- and dumbbell-shaped crystals. She reports regular vitamin C supplementation.
question: Which of the following is the most likely type of stone and an appropriate preventive treatment?

options.text: Uric acid stone; alkalinization of urine and allopurinol
Struvite stone; eradication of infection and surgical removal
Calcium oxalate stone; thiazides, citrate, and a low-sodium diet
Cystine stone; low-sodium diet and chelating agents
Calcium phosphate stone; urine alkalinization alone

explanation_correct: Calcium stones account for about 80% of kidney stones, and calcium oxalate is more common than calcium phosphate. Calcium oxalate stones are radiopaque and hyperdense on CT with envelope- or dumbbell-shaped crystals. Causes include ethylene glycol ingestion, vitamin C overuse, hypocitraturia, and malabsorption (eg, Crohn disease). Treatment and prevention include thiazides, citrate, and a low-sodium diet.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uric acid stones are radiolucent with rhomboid/rosette crystals, form in acidic urine, and are linked to gout or high cell turnover, not envelope crystals or vitamin C use.
explanation_incorrect.B: Struvite stones are staghorn calculi with coffin-lid crystals caused by urease-producing bacterial infection, not by vitamin C supplementation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cystine stones are hexagonal and faintly radiopaque, begin in childhood from an autosomal recessive transporter defect, and are not related to vitamin C.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calcium phosphate stones are wedge-shaped prisms associated with high urine pH and are treated with thiazides and a low-sodium diet, not urine alkalinization alone.

educationalObjective: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common, radiopaque with envelope/dumbbell crystals, and prevented with thiazides, citrate, and low sodium.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 40-year-old man with recurrent kidney stones has radiopaque, hyperdense stones on imaging. Urine microscopy shows wedge-shaped prism crystals, and his urine pH is persistently elevated.
question: Which of the following best identifies this stone and its recommended treatment?

options.text: Calcium phosphate stone; low-sodium diet and thiazides
Uric acid stone; alkalinization of urine
Cystine stone; chelating agents
Struvite stone; surgical removal only
Calcium oxalate stone; vitamin C restriction alone

explanation_correct: Calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque and hyperdense with wedge-shaped prism crystals and are associated with high urine pH. Calcium stones overall make up about 80% of stones. Treatment includes a low-sodium diet and thiazides. This distinguishes them from calcium oxalate stones, which are linked to hypocitraturia and lower urine pH and form envelope/dumbbell crystals.

explanation_incorrect.B: Uric acid stones are radiolucent rhomboid/rosette crystals that form in acidic urine and are treated with alkalinization and allopurinol, not wedge-shaped radiopaque crystals.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cystine stones are hexagonal, faintly radiopaque stones from an inherited transporter defect; chelating agents are reserved for refractory cystinuria, not high-pH wedge crystals.
explanation_incorrect.D: Struvite stones are radiopaque coffin-lid crystals from urease-producing infection and require eradication of infection plus surgical removal, not removal alone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calcium oxalate stones form envelope/dumbbell crystals; vitamin C overuse is a cause of oxalate stones, so restriction alone would not address this wedge-shaped, high-pH stone.

educationalObjective: Calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque wedge-shaped prisms associated with high urine pH and treated with thiazides and low sodium.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent urinary tract infections and a large branching renal stone on imaging that fills the renal pelvis. Urine pH is alkaline, and microscopy shows coffin-lid (sarcophagus) crystals. Culture grows Proteus mirabilis.
question: Which of the following best explains this stone's formation and management?

options.text: Uric acid stone from hyperuricemia; treated with allopurinol
Calcium oxalate stone from hypocitraturia; treated with citrate
Cystine stone from a PCT transporter defect; treated with chelators
Calcium phosphate stone from high urine pH; treated with thiazides
Struvite stone from urease-producing bacteria causing urine alkalinization; treat the infection and remove the stone surgically

explanation_correct: Struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) stones account for about 15% of stones and are caused by infection with urease-positive organisms such as Proteus mirabilis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and Klebsiella. These bacteria hydrolyze urea to ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and promoting stone formation. They are radiopaque, hyperdense, coffin-lid shaped, and commonly form staghorn calculi. Treatment is eradication of the underlying infection and surgical removal of the stone.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uric acid stones are radiolucent rhomboid/rosette crystals that form in acidic urine with gout or leukemia; they are not infection-related staghorn stones.
explanation_incorrect.B: Calcium oxalate stones are envelope/dumbbell crystals linked to hypocitraturia, vitamin C, or ethylene glycol, not urease-producing bacterial infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cystine stones are hexagonal, faintly radiopaque stones from an autosomal recessive PCT transporter defect beginning in childhood, not from a Proteus infection.
explanation_incorrect.D: Calcium phosphate stones are wedge-shaped prisms associated with high urine pH but are not caused by urease-producing organisms or treated by infection eradication.

educationalObjective: Struvite staghorn stones form from urease-producing bacterial infection with alkaline urine and coffin-lid crystals; treat infection plus surgical removal.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 60-year-old man with gout has colicky flank pain and a radiolucent renal stone on imaging. Urine microscopy shows rhomboid and rosette-shaped crystals, and his urine pH is low.
question: Which of the following is the most likely stone and its treatment?

options.text: Calcium oxalate stone; thiazides
Struvite stone; antibiotics and surgery
Cystine stone; low-sodium diet
Uric acid stone; alkalinization of urine and allopurinol
Calcium phosphate stone; thiazides

explanation_correct: Uric acid stones make up about 5% of stones, are radiolucent (one of the two 'I can't see you' stones), and form in acidic urine with rhomboid or rosette crystals. They are strongly associated with hyperuricemia (eg, gout) and diseases with increased cell turnover (eg, leukemia). Treatment is alkalinization of the urine and allopurinol.

explanation_incorrect.A: Calcium oxalate stones are radiopaque envelope/dumbbell crystals, not radiolucent rhomboid crystals associated with gout.
explanation_incorrect.B: Struvite stones are radiopaque coffin-lid staghorn stones from urease-producing infection and require antibiotics plus surgical removal, not alkalinization and allopurinol.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cystine stones are hexagonal and faintly radiopaque, begin in childhood from a transporter defect, and are not associated with gout or hyperuricemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque wedge-shaped prisms seen with high urine pH, not low pH radiolucent stones in a patient with gout.

educationalObjective: Uric acid stones are radiolucent, rhomboid/rosette crystals in acidic urine with gout or high cell turnover; treat with alkalinization and allopurinol.

subject: Renal
vignette: An 11-year-old boy has had recurrent stones since childhood. The stones are faintly radiopaque, and a staghorn calculus is seen. Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals; the sodium cyanide nitroprusside test is positive. Genetic testing shows an autosomal recessive defect in a proximal tubule transporter.
question: Which of the following best explains the defect and the additional amino acids affected?

options.text: Defective uric acid transporter with elevated uric acid; associated with gout
Defective cystine-reabsorbing PCT transporter (cystinuria) with poor reabsorption of ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA)
Defective calcium oxalate handling with hypercalciuria; associated with hypocitraturia
Urease-producing bacterial infection alkalinizing urine; associated with Proteus mirabilis
Defective phosphate excretion with high urine pH; associated with wedge-shaped crystals

explanation_correct: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive condition in which the cystine-reabsorbing proximal tubule transporter loses function, causing cystine stones. The same transporter defect causes poor reabsorption of ornithine, lysine, and arginine (mnemonic COLA). Cystine is poorly soluble, so stones form, usually beginning in childhood; they may be staghorn and are faintly radiopaque with a positive sodium cyanide nitroprusside test. Treatment includes low sodium, alkalinization, and chelating agents (tiopronin, penicillamine) if refractory.

explanation_incorrect.A: A uric acid transporter problem would produce radiolucent rhomboid stones in acidic urine with hyperuricemia, not hexagonal faintly radiopaque childhood stones with a positive cyanide nitroprusside test.
explanation_incorrect.C: Calcium oxalate handling errors produce radiopaque envelope/dumbbell crystals in adults, not hexagonal crystals or a defect in amino acid reabsorption.
explanation_incorrect.D: Urease-producing bacteria cause struvite stones with coffin-lid crystals and alkaline urine, not an inherited proximal tubule amino acid transporter defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Defective phosphate excretion producing wedge-shaped radiopaque crystals describes calcium phosphate stones, which are not associated with the COLA amino acids.

educationalObjective: Cystinuria is an AR PCT cystine transporter defect with hexagonal, faintly radiopaque childhood stones and impaired reabsorption of ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA).

subject: Renal
vignette: A plain abdominal radiograph fails to visualize a renal stone in a patient with hematuria and colicky flank pain. The mnemonic 'I can't see you' is being used to recall which stones are radiolucent.
question: Which of the following pairs of stones is radiolucent?

options.text: Calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate
Struvite and calcium phosphate
Cystine and uric acid
Calcium oxalate and struvite
Calcium phosphate and uric acid

explanation_correct: The two stones recalled by the mnemonic 'I can't c (see) u (you)' are cystine and uric acid, which are radiolucent on imaging (cystine is at most faintly radiopaque). Calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque and hyperdense on CT, and struvite stones are also radiopaque. Radiolucency explains why a plain film may miss these stones.

explanation_incorrect.A: Both calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque and hyperdense on CT, so neither is a radiolucent stone.
explanation_incorrect.B: Struvite stones are radiopaque and calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque; neither is visualized poorly on plain film in this mnemonic.
explanation_incorrect.D: Calcium oxalate stones are radiopaque and struvite stones are radiopaque, so this pair does not match the mnemonic.
explanation_incorrect.E: Uric acid is radiolucent, but calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque, so this pair is only half correct.

educationalObjective: Cystine and uric acid are the radiolucent stones ('I can't see you'); calcium and struvite stones are radiopaque.
source: Generated from 14. Renal.pdf - Pathology: Kidney stones

subject: Renal
vignette: A 38-year-old man has a ureteral stone causing acute unilateral obstruction. He has flank tenderness, colicky pain radiating to the groin, and hematuria.
question: Which of the following are serious complications that can result from obstructive stones if left untreated?

options.text: Hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, and acute kidney injury
Nephrotic syndrome, renal vein thrombosis, and hypoalbuminemia
Renal tubular acidosis, hypokalemia, and spontaneous stone dissolution
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescent formation
Bladder outlet obstruction, detrusor underactivity, and overflow incontinence

explanation_correct: Kidney stones can lead to severe complications including hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, and acute kidney injury when they obstruct urine flow. An obstructed stone classically presents with unilateral flank tenderness, colicky pain radiating to the groin, and hematuria. Encouraging fluid intake is central to both treatment and prevention.

explanation_incorrect.B: Nephrotic syndrome with renal vein thrombosis and hypoalbuminemia is a glomerular disease (classically membranous nephropathy), not a complication of obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Renal tubular acidosis and hypokalemia are tubular disorders, and stones do not spontaneously dissolve as a consequence of obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Crescentic rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is a nephritic immune-mediated process, not a mechanical complication of a stone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bladder outlet obstruction and detrusor underactivity cause overflow incontinence, not the obstructive complications of a ureteral stone.

educationalObjective: Obstructive stones can cause hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, and AKI; presentation is unilateral colicky flank pain with hematuria.

subject: Renal
vignette: A pathology review asks residents to match each kidney stone type with its urine crystal morphology and radiographic appearance.
question: Which of the following stone-type and crystal/radiographic pairings is correct?

options.text: Uric acid — envelope-shaped crystals, radiopaque
Struvite — rhomboid crystals, radiolucent
Calcium oxalate — hexagonal crystals, faintly radiopaque
Calcium phosphate — coffin-lid crystals, radiopaque
Cystine — hexagonal crystals, faintly radiopaque

explanation_correct: Cystine stones are hexagonal ('sixtine' stones) and faintly radiopaque with moderately radiodense CT appearance, beginning in childhood and associated with a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test. By contrast, uric acid stones are rhomboid/rosette and radiolucent, struvite stones are coffin-lid and radiopaque, calcium oxalate stones are envelope/dumbbell and radiopaque, and calcium phosphate stones are wedge-shaped prisms and radiopaque.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uric acid stones are rhomboid or rosette shaped and radiolucent, not envelope-shaped and radiopaque; envelope/dumbbell crystals are calcium oxalate.
explanation_incorrect.B: Struvite stones form radiopaque coffin-lid crystals from urease-producing infection; rhomboid radiolucent crystals are uric acid.
explanation_incorrect.C: Calcium oxalate stones are envelope- or dumbbell-shaped and radiopaque; hexagonal faintly radiopaque crystals are cystine.
explanation_incorrect.D: Calcium phosphate stones are wedge-shaped prisms and radiopaque; coffin-lid crystals are characteristic of struvite stones.

educationalObjective: Pairings: cystine hexagonal/faintly radiopaque, uric acid rhomboid/radiolucent, struvite coffin-lid/radiopaque, calcium oxalate envelope/radiopaque, calcium phosphate wedge/radiopaque.
